passage:
Monday: Nikita and her friends planned to bunk the last period and go to the mall food court. "You're coming, Sharmila, right?" Sharmila laughed and said, "Maybe," though her stomach dropped.
Wednesday: She went. She spent the whole afternoon looking at her phone, expecting a call from school. The food tasted of nothing.
The next Monday: When they planned it again, Sharmila said, "I'm out. It's not my thing." Nikita rolled her eyes. "Boring." Sharmila shrugged, though her hands were cold. Two days later Nikita sat next to her in the library and asked quietly how she'd said no so easily. "It wasn't easy," Sharmila said.

qa.q: Where did the group go when they bunked?
qa.a: To the mall food court.

qa.q: Why did the food taste of nothing to Sharmila?
qa.a: She was anxious about being caught and uncomfortable doing something that didn't feel like her.

qa.q: What helped Sharmila say no the second time?
qa.a: She had already felt how wrong it was for her, so she could name it simply: "It's not my thing."

qa.q: What does Nikita's question in the library suggest about her?
qa.a: She may feel the pressure too and quietly admire Sharmila for resisting it.

grounding: It shows a teenager going along with group pressure once, then choosing to act as herself.

passage: Nilesh, I'll tell you about the worst day of my Class 11. My friends decided to make fun of a boy who stammered. They wanted me to imitate him during break, because I was good at voices. Everyone was waiting. "Come on, Manoj." My mouth went dry. I wanted to be the funny one; I also knew it was cruel. I said, "Not this," and walked off to the canteen. For a week they called me boring and didn't save me a seat. I ate alone. But on the fourth day the boy found me there and sat down without a word. We're still friends. I don't regret losing that seat.

qa.q: What did the friends want young Manoj to do?
qa.a: Imitate a boy who stammered during break.

qa.q: What was young Manoj feeling when his mouth went dry?
qa.a: Torn between wanting to be the funny one his friends admired and knowing the joke was cruel.

qa.q: What does Manoj's story show about the cost of standing firm?
qa.a: There can be a real price, like a week of eating alone, but it can also bring truer friendships.

qa.q: How might the boy who stammered have felt when he sat beside Manoj?
qa.a: Grateful and safe, recognising someone who had refused to mock him.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a teenager choosing their own values over intense pressure to go along with the group.

passage: It was eleven at night before the chemistry board exam, and the group video call was buzzing. Jatin said someone had "the paper" and was sharing a link. "Everyone's doing it, Rashmi. Don't be stupid." Rashmi's heart was pounding. She was tired, the power had just gone off, and her notes were half-revised by torchlight. Part of her wanted the link just to stop feeling behind. But she thought about the version of herself she liked: the one who earned her marks. "I'm going to sleep," she said. "Good luck." She left the call, set her alarm for five and revised by candlelight in the morning. The "paper" turned out to be fake. Half the call had studied the wrong questions.

qa.q: When was the group call?
qa.a: At eleven at night, before the chemistry board exam.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi tempted by the link?
qa.a: She was tired, behind in revision and the power had gone, so the link promised relief from feeling unprepared.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi resist the pressure?
qa.a: She thought about the kind of person she wanted to be and left the call, then used a practical plan of an early alarm.

qa.q: How might Jatin and the others feel the next day?
qa.a: Panicked and regretful, having wasted time on a fake paper while Rashmi revised.

grounding: It shows a teenager holding on to her own values against strong peer pressure at a stressful moment.

passage: The whole gang in Samir's colony in Hyderabad got the same buzz cut the week before term started. 'Your turn tomorrow,' they told him at the gate. Samir, fifteen, had been growing his curls since summer; he liked tying them back when he played the tabla. That night he stood in front of the mirror, pulling the curls straight, trying to picture himself without them. His neighbour Kashish, sixteen, out walking her dog, saw him on the steps later. 'You look like someone going to a punishment.' 'They're all doing it.' 'Do you want to?' He took a long time to answer. 'I want them to stop calling me the different one.' Next morning he went to the barber, asked for just a trim, and walked to the gate with his heart thumping.

qa.q: What instrument does Samir play?
qa.a: He plays the tabla.

qa.q: What did Samir's answer to Kashish show about what he wanted?
qa.a: He didn't want the haircut itself; he wanted to stop being singled out, so he felt torn between belonging and staying himself.

qa.q: What could help Samir if the group teases him about the trim?
qa.a: He could answer lightly and confidently, and spend time with people like Kashish who accept him as he is.

qa.q: What would change if Samir's friends had treated the haircut as optional?
qa.a: He could keep his curls without feeling he was risking his place in the group.

grounding: Shows a teenager torn between keeping his own look and matching his friends, and choosing his own way.

passage:
'Rajni, the group decided. Black dresses, all nine of us, for the farewell photo.'
'I heard.' Rajni kept folding Nani's green saree on the bed.
Mumma, from the doorway: 'That's the one you wanted to wear, na?'
'Wanted.'
Vandana sat down beside her. 'You'll look like the odd one out in the photo.'
'I know.'
'So?'
'So I've been thinking about it for three days.' Rajni ran her thumb along the border. 'Nani wore this to her own farewell. I wanted to wear it to mine.'
Mumma said nothing, which Rajni knew was deliberate.
Vandana sighed. 'What if you wear it for the function and change for the group photo?'
'That's... not bad.' Rajni looked up. 'Or I wear it the whole time and stand in the middle.'
Vandana laughed. 'Okay, bold. I'll stand next to you.'

qa.q: Who wore the green saree to her own farewell?
qa.a: Nani wore it to her own farewell.

qa.q: What does Rajni running her thumb along the border suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels torn, deeply attached to the saree and to Nani yet pulled by the wish to fit in with the group.

qa.q: How did Mumma support Rajni in this scene?
qa.a: She reminded her of what she had wanted and then stayed quiet, leaving the decision to Rajni.

qa.q: How does Vandana's view change during the talk?
qa.a: She starts by warning Rajni she will stand out, then offers a compromise and finally chooses to stand beside her.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager weighing her own wish against her group's plan to match, with her friend and mother present.
